content:
I used GPT to formalize Chen’s theorem in Lean 4: every sufficiently large even integer is a prime plus either a prime or a product of two primes—the “1+2” result toward Goldbach.

Code: https://github.com/subfish-zhou/goldbach-lean

No sorry or unproved mathematical assumptions beyond Lean’s standard classical axioms. The theorem passed the official Lean Comparator checks, and I gave it a brief manual review. I then asked GPT to clean up and rebuild the project. Hopefully it’s readable. Reviews and independent checks are welcome.

233,282 lines of code across 729 Lean modules, excluding comments and blank lines but including adapted upstream code. With dependencies cached, a clean project build took 36m 23s and about 6 GiB of sampled peak memory, with shared pages counted proportionally, on my Xeon server (LEAN_NUM_THREADS=2).

I started on August 19, with my Hermes Agent writing proofs and coordinating Copilot. GPT-5.6-sol handled the work until today; GPT-6-astra handled the final stretch.

Detailed Costs:

GPT-5.6-sol-fast:
Input 288,848,118 Cache Read 7,563,242,033
Output 27,762,455 Cache Write 102,454,384
GPT-6:
Input 20,031,610 Cache Read 631,011,633
Output 2,840,891 Cache Write 16,938,413

Roughly 90% of the main proof package’s final code volume was in place before the model switch; about 10% was added afterward.

We did not formalize Chen’s 1973 proof line by line. The route combines switching arguments, weighted linear and Selberg sieves, modern treatments by Suzuki and Liu, and Bombieri–Vinogradov/Pan-type distribution estimates.

We reused and extended UyNewNas’s Chen and analytic-number-theory code, and built on Mathlib and PrimeNumberTheoremAnd

Next is Jiamin Li and Jianya Liu’s “1+1.9” theorem, first posted on June 1, 2026 and revised on August 8. For every sufficiently large even N, it gives N = p + rq, with p and q prime, r either 1 or prime, and r ≤ q^0.9.

I expect to add 1+1.9 soon. I also want to formalize the 1+1.894 refinement the authors mention using Wu’s double sieve but do not work out in detail.

Could this be a good starting point for AI to eventually solve Goldbach’s conjecture?
Congrats! This is different from the (private) submission by Cond-t at LeanEval on September 1, right?

Junyan Xu said:

Congrats! This is different from the (private) submission by Cond-t at LeanEval on September 1, right?

I have no idea about this submission.

From Chen’s 1+2 to Li–Liu’s 1+1.9! We’ve verified in Lean 4 the biggest breakthrough on the Goldbach conjecture in 60 years!
Li–Liu’s paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05224 Congratulations to the authors!
Formalization project: https://subfish-zhou.github.io/goldbach-lean/

I’m sharing this formal verification result as soon as it’s ready. I’ll continue refining this rough initial formalization to make it shorter, faster, and more readable, while keeping the documentation up to date.
We’d love your feedback and contributions!
Interesting! Do you have any plan formalizing Yitang Zhang's work on Siegel zero?
I'd like to first build a comprehensive, high-quality library for analytic number theory. I am currently reorganizing and optimizing 1+1.9 and primegap186 as a good starting point.
